content.title: The biggest what-if in running history
content.text: On Nov. 2, I had my social media feeds — welcomely — inundated with New York City Marathon posts. Of those posts, there was one particular video that stuck out. It was of a grown adult man moved to tears as he watched legendary marathoner Eliud Kipchoge compete in his final World Marathon Major.I hesitate to call myself a marathoner, considering I’ve only ran one single marathon, yet every time I watch this video I begin to tear up. The distance, as arbitrary and ridiculous as it is, strikes an emotional chord with the human experience of triumph, defeat and everything in between. My immediate and consistent emotional response to these videos caused me to think: Why is it that this specific race carries so much more emotional weight? What makes this strange and honestly insane practice an emotional spectacle for both runners and non-runners? Fortescue's Forrest Urges Quick US-Iran Off-RampWhile I believe that some semblance of that answer is based on how hard it is to run a marathon at the limits of your capabilities, I also believe that more of it is about what the distance represents. Running 26.2 miles is hard. Making a decision to spend hundreds of dollars and hours to go out and be in excruciating pain is hard. Yet, people do it for that exact reason: It’s difficult. Deciding to do hard things is a way to express your enduring self-belief. To succeed, you must tell yourself, “I will now achieve this, because of and in spite of my feelings about it.”That’s why, as I tear up to this viral TikTok, I believe the video of Kipchoge resonates so much emotionally. The marathon is the ultimate test of seeing what you can become if you really work hard at something. Kipchoge’s “no human is limited” catchphrase is an epitome of the self-belief that comes with doing these difficult challenges.However, for almost the entirety of the 26.2-mile distance’s history, there was a limiting metric. Running a marathon in under 2 hours was considered impossible. Many had tried, and all had failed. This was until Kipchoge teamed up with the company Ineos to produce the perfect conditions to run a sub-two-hour marathon. With the assistance of laser-timed pace vehicles, 41 rotating runners blocking the wind and delivery of hydration and nutrition via bicycle, Kipchoge broke the tape at 1:59:40. This required an entirely inconceivable 4:33-per-mile pace. I, a mere mortal, ran a 2:59:39 marathon last December in my one and only marathon (so far). In the peak shape of my life, it’d be very unlikely I could run a single mile at a 4:33 pace, let alone 26.Kipchoge’s triumph was the fastest marathon ever run by a human being, proving that indeed, no human is limited. However, due to the outside aid and lack of competition, his feat didn’t count as the world record. But it challenged the idea that the goalposts of an “official” sub-two-hour marathon as the new metric were immovable. And it seemed to be a new immovable time. Until Kelvin Kiptum came on the scene and gave Kipchoge a run for his money.Kiptum made his pro marathon debut in 2022, shocking the world by running a 2:01:53 at the Valencia Marathon. This was the fastest debut in history and fourth fastest time ever.He swiftly followed up that insanity by breaking the tape of the 2022 London Marathon in 2:01:25, the second-fastest marathon of all time, second to Kipchoge’s official personal record of 2:01:09.Most impressive of all, Kiptum broke the brains of running fans across the world when he set his fastest time on the legendary course of the 2023 Chicago Marathon, running 2:00:35 for a new world record.I remember seeing this metric online and thinking to myself, “He’s going to break two hours.” Kipchoge had laid the groundwork that running that speed was possible, and Kiptum had the incredible genetic makeup to achieve it in competition. Yet, the beauty of the marathon is also what can make it so devastating. The distance itself becomes a reflection of potential. Such joy and achievement can come from the race, but also such loss.Just three months after his world record marathon, Kelvin Kiptum died at the age of 24 in a car crash in his home country of Kenya on Feb. 11, 2024. This news understandably leveled the running world. A man, younger than I am now, was taken from the world. Someone who was on the brink of achieving a metric representative of the indomitable human spirit to achieve and succeed. And a loss like this cannot be examined only within the marathon world. It’s unfair to regard Kiptum as just a runner. He represented what was possible in a sport that has an intrinsic connection with the human spirit. That’s why I regard Kiptum’s death as easily the biggest what-if in distance running history, arguably in sports history. Kiptum had plans to run the Rotterdam Marathon, and had publicly stated he was going to attempt to break the unachievable two-hour mark. And I, for one, believed that he would have done it on that day.Marathon running is many things — cliches and all — but I believe that above all else, it embodies what it means to be human. It’s human to give yourself a goal that is seemingly impossible, and scratch and claw your way to realizing it. It’s human to feel the jubilation that comes with reaching your goal and to feel the devastation that comes with falling short. And it’s human, more than anything, to wonder what could have been.
